It was primarily instant mashed potatoes above a ground beef gruel. I counted 5 peas. There was little beef and mostly a gravy-like substance beneath the top layer. Pathetic. 

I made the best of it, and did not request a better meal. I don't like being that guy. Still, it showed that Tuby Ruesday was willing to sell overpriced garbage dishes without qualms for quality nor their reputation. 

If they don't care what they offer their customers, neither will we care to find out what comes next. In this business, one strike is all you get.

Complete ripoff.

I just checked the Village Bagel website to confirm what I had read before; "...You will not be disappointed...Stop by..."

Well, when I arrived at their shop after a 30 minute drive from home to sample their product, I followed the directions posted on their windows to call in an order. No problem. Happy to comply. 

Unfortunately, the friendly sounding woman on the line advised me that they were not conducting any retail business for the day, but only filling orders for Christmas. I could not walk in, nor order a breakfast bagel (onion w garden veggie & coffee), but would have to leave empty handed. Not even explaining my long drive, nor the absence of any notice on their website, let alone, Yelp, nor sign on their front door, could persuade her to extend a humanitarian exception and slice/smear a bagel for me. 

Nope. I would have to drive away without satisfaction. 

Ho hum...

Merry Christmas to you, too! 

There wasn't any room at the inn, either. At least I am in good company.

Shumai Wok is a new entry to the "Asian Fusion" takeout wars in Penndel, Pa. It is one of those places that really only does "to go" food, although there is a solitary table sitting there for those like me who want to eat before returning to the office.  It is also one of those pseudo-fusion joints that offers Chinese, Japanese, and Thai dishes on their menu, but are really just a low budget Chinese house that makes cheap inauthentic versions of Japanese and Thai food, and does a sushi business in an attempt to be all things to all people.  

While I cannot speak to the sushi, I did recently have a dish of Pad Thai with Chicken, which as a lunch special came with a choice of Soup and Rice.  As Thai soups were not offered, I accepted Wonton and Pork Fried Rice as the complements to the meal. Strange combo.  

Of course, although I was eating there, everything came to the table in take out containers.  Okay. I can deal with that.  The Wonton Soup was overly salty (MSG?), and the wontons themselves, thick and without much filling.  The Fried Rice was dyed yellow from the chicken broth it was cook in that morning, was al dente and not worth the calories.  Finally, the Pad Thai used the wrong thin noodles, and a sauce that tasted like the topping for General Tso's Chicken, not the traditional gravy that a Thai kitchen would produce.  The weird orange color gave it away.  

This was a one time only visit.  Although the people who work there (owners) are friendly and the prices are low, the food was a major downer, and it seems impossible for it to get to neutral ground where it would be tolerable.

Sad to say, the other reviewers are correct. 
This is an example of how a bad business can continue to thrive in the absence of competition.  It is obvious the workers reflect the attitude of the management.  They make half hearted attempts to do the job, although they appear to be swarming over the car with sprays and rags.  There is always something left undone, and nary a smile or "thank you for coming."

Mallu Cafe on Verree just off Bustleton in far Northeast Philly is really a take out Indian joint, with a few tables for those who don't mind the run down decor or aren't aware of the business model employed (like me). Their website was interesting, and showed nice photos of many of their Kerala dishes. Perhaps, I should have been deterred by the sketchy dudes hanging by the front door (even more of them when we left), but they smiled when we approached and invited us in. 

Strange, but no big deal.

We ordered Chicken 65 (spicy chili fried), Avial (mixed veggie coconut curry) and Appam (rice flour fry bread). They arrived in take out containers with plastic forks (?!). The chicken had been deep fried to a very dark brown and delivered without any sauce. Obviously, overcooked by someone who didn't know their own recipe, or hadn't looked at their website, as I had. I returned it to the kitchen. I wanted it done the right way, but that wasn't offered. Rather, they wanted to give us Kerala Chicken Curry. 

Okay. Whatever.

While we waited we sampled the veggie dish. It was cool on top and hot at the base. Microwaved, and no one bothered to see if it was fully recooked. Nope. Further, it didn't look like the pics on the website, either. Rather than having distinct veggies, it was all mashed together. Didn't change the decent taste, but the presentation was lacking. 

When the replacement curry arrived we quickly saw that it was bone in small pieces. Hard to deal with only a plastic fork. The flavor was fine, but with the morsels to contend with it was not worth the effort. It was hard to understand why they would give us the bones, when boneless was only a buck more. Besides, they never asked which we would prefer. No. My sense was they were annoyed about their earlier mistake with the 65, knew they could not charge us for that, and decided to throw some shade at us by literally boning us. 

We surrendered, asked for the check, and definitely did not want to take anything home. 

When we left there were more dudes just hanging around outside. Maybe they were waiting for us to leave so they could start their pinochle game. 

Mallu Cafe just didn't seem to be a restaurant anymore. There are plenty of good Indian houses in this part of the city. This place just isn't one of them. 

1 Star - Avoid

The was a reason why this BK was practically empty when I stopped in for a quick breakfast the other day.  

The Biscuit for my sandwich was hard and too small to enclose its contents.  It appeared to be a tube biscuit that had been made earlier and left in the open air to dry out, and then microwaved just before sale.  It rehardened quickly and was a crumbly mess to eat.  Just not very good, despite the fact that the rest of the ingredients seemed fresh.  

Given the competition across the street, it is difficult to see how this place survives. Maybe their burgers are better, but I won't be back to find out.

It pains me to remember the recently completed dinner at Taco Suave.  Such high expectations after reading the other reviews.  Such auspicious beginnings. Such a sudden and disappointing finale.

We walked in to this tiny strip mall corner restaurant. About a dozen tables with white table clothes.  I was thinking that in my experience, the hole in the wall Mexican joints were always the best.  At least, that had been true in Arizona, New Mexico, Colorado and even SoCal. 

 We sat and ordered the Agua de Pina (Pineapple Water), which was a first and a pleasant drink of diluted pineapple juice whipped to a froth.  Really good! I was getting more excited as I imagined we had just discovered the Fountain of Youth drink right here in Warrington.  Then the homemade Chips and Fresh Salsa came out. Heavy crunchy mild oily sensation with a mild Mexi flavor, and a Tomato, Cilantro Salsa with a sweetness equal to the chili's heat.  Loved it. 

Encouraged and feeling adventurous by the fun of the apps and drink, I went for the Pollo Dorado (Golden Fried Chicken), the most expensive item on the menu.  Visions of plump chicken breast with a wonderful fruity sauce danced in my head. My friends had a Burrito de Carne Asada, and a Taco con Queso.  

What was placed before me was instead three over cooked deep fried drumsticks with an oil soaked brown coating that tasted primarily of salt.  My physical reaction to eating this was matched by the instantly deflated sense of gluttony so rudely assaulted and kicked to the curb.  I kept eating hoping for a secondary burst of flavor to save this.  It did not come. I passed around the chicken and the reaction was universal. Bad. 

The Burrito de Carne Asada was large and full of bits of beef and cheese, but way too mild, and a bit too fatty.  It was left one third eaten.  The Taco con Queso presented well, but was practically tasteless.  We liberally added hot salsa to throw them life preservers, but we could not save them.  The dinner was a victim of drowning. 

We will not be back.  I wish I had a different review to write about Taco Suave, but true to the Yelpers Creed, I cannot hide from the bitter taste of a disappointing meal.  

Our server, Mirna, was great!

The Blue Duck is a nice place to stop for brunch or lunch if you find yourself in the vicinity.  It has a reputation for offering "Center City" atmosphere, with "Northeast Philly" earthiness.  I guess that means you don't always have to run downtown to find a cool place to eat, or conversely, that Northeast Philly now has its own duck fat fries outlet.  Can I hear a, "Hallelujah!"?

We stopped in for a late lunch after an appointment with Homeland Security on Drummond Road nearby.  That is never a sparkling experience, and we all wanted something to wash away the bureaucratic dust that comes with dealing with the Feds. We ordered three of their signature burgers, and the Salt & Pepper Fries for the table.  Water all around. We waited about 20 minutes for our meals to arrive, all the while smelling the grilling beef in the open kitchen.  This was a very hot day, and the HVAC was struggling to maintain the right comfort level.  Even with the front door closed, the humidity in the house was noticeable.  

The House Grind Burger, Pork Roll Burger and Beast of Northeast Burger arrived in the arms of our erstwhile server.  All looked great with Brioche-style rolls, and the individual toppings.  My Beast was a mix of Wild Boar and Beef, Smoked Gouda, Sweet Tomato Jam, Bacon and Crisp Sriracha Shoestring Onions.  Beautiful to behold.  First bite should have been awesome, but aside from the interesting flavor of the fixings, the "Medium" finish requested was in fact, "Well Done."  With the juice gone, I could not taste the difference in the meats, and found the burger less than hoped. The same was true for the House Grind, although for some reason the Pork Roll Burger came out "Medium Rare,"  and amply juiced.  The S & P Fries were good; hot, but not crisp. 

It is always awkward to low rank a popular restaurant, but it was what it was.  Someone needs to pay more attention at the grill, as it is likely to have happened before.  

Good luck with your new Center City enterprise.

I am about to give up on Frozen Yogurt joints. 

Over the last year or more, I have not found a single one that offers a quality product that tastes as good as the equivalent ice cream.  While it is nice to save on calories (if that is really the case), tasteless extrusions just don't satisfy my need for something cold, creamy and sweet.  

This Redberry, while small and clean, offers nothing better than the others.  The Traditional Vanilla and Peanut Butter choices were indistinguishable from each other.  Only the add ons had any taste. 

What's the point?

For a place that specializes in one thing - salad - there is a disconnect between their mission and final product. 

 I have eaten here a few times over the years, and while nothing I have ordered/eaten has been bad, my impression was that the bowls were thrown together by rote with excessive inattention to detail.  Often the ingredients are just dropped into the salad bowl and left unmixed or given a perfunctory stir.  Separate piles of cheese, nuts, dried fruits, etc., left where they fall.  Sometimes, one of the elements is forgotten without awareness of the shortcoming.  

When the pleasure of this experience comes in over $10 for lunch, it is difficult to think that value has been attained.  Asking for the dressing on the side to take charge of the finish is helpful, but when it becomes necessary to insure that I am dealing with a salad and not piles of vegetables as yet unrelated to each other, I feel like I am doing their jobs. 

With so many other restaurants offering healthy creative fresh salads as part of a broader menu, there seems little reason to go to a place whose sole reason for existence is doing something that is ultimately inferior to the competition.  There is something inherently contradictory in a mass produced "custom made" salad.  

That contradiction is manifest by what comes across the counter at Saladworks.

BREAKFAST TAKE OUT REVIEW

We had an office meeting in Norristown, PA, this morning. Our office manager took our requests for breakfast and ordered everything from nearby Pauline's Deli. There were eight of us.  I asked for a sausage, egg and cheese sandwich on toasted English muffin. 

When I arrived I sat at the conference table with an aluminum foil wrapped package before me. It was still warm. Upon opening, I quickly realized that I had a pork roll, egg and cheese on English, not what I had requested. This may not have been Pauline's doing, as I looked around and noticed my associate had a very similar sandwich, but with sausage. It was too late to make the exchange, as he was already happily half way through MY SANDWICH. For the sake of team building, I said nothing.

I am not a pork roll guy. Don't care for the taste, nor the texture. Still, I suffered through it, and drowned my disappointment in the hot coffee made in our office. 

Better labeling might solve this kind of mix up, and a closer examination by the consumer would certainly be a benefit. I realize that it may not be fair to say Pauline messed this up, but I really didn't care for the sandwich. Hopefully, I'll get another chance at the next breakfast session, and be able to judge what I actually wanted. 

YELP Suggestion - There should be a box to check for take out reviews. It isn't close to equivalent to evaluate a dining in experience with a take away bite. I quickly stop reading take out reviews as being irrelevant to the quality and enjoyability of the exact same meal eaten in these two divergent circumstances.

As McDonald's go, this one on West Trenton Avenue in Morrisville, Pa., is in the format of a modern smaller footprint, with a drive through that wraps tightly around the building, forcing pedestrians to cross this lane of traffic. With all the young people who frequent these kid magnets, you would think they could find a safer design.  Alas, not. 

I stopped in the other morning when traffic heading over the Delaware was so bad I decided to find a rest stop to wait for the clogged artery that is the Calhoun Street Bridge to pass its blockage.  Mickey's was right there, so I went in.  The place was clean and a little busy. Still, my order was taken promptly.  I had to wait a while for it to be filled as the staff seemed to lack any real organization for the counter.  The six people I saw all had their backs turned to the customers, and when any one of them was free and looked around to see us there, they carried out the next step in the process.  Three different people worked on my order.  I finally realized that what I was observing was the result of the heavy drive thru business which kept everyone's attention, and left those of us inside as forgotten players in their fast food game.  Efficient, perhaps, but not given to warm face to face. 

My Sausage, Egg and Cheese Biscuit was smallish, and thrown together in such a way the top of the biscuit adhered to the cheese to one side of the sandwich, leaving the rest exposed.  It was wrapped and bagged that way, and made the eating a bit awkward. I guess if this product had gone to a drive away customer, by the time it was opened, they would be too far away to do anything but grumble.  Another casualty to the dominance of drive thru culture. 

For me, I was just disappointed with the lack of care in the work product, and knew that I wasn't coming back for another round of being ignored.  

Oh. The coffee was good.

Not sure the last time RJ's boiled and baked the bagels in the bins, but as I am eating one less than 30 minutes after purchase @ 1:00 pm on a Sunday, it is already approaching staleness. Too flat upon observation; a tough slice with a sharp serrated knife; tough crust with no crispness; and too dense at its heart.  
Very ordinary. 
Bagel Train is far superior to my taste.

Great Shanghai Chinese Restaurant in the Morrisville Plaza Shopping Center is another primarily take out shop that has been around for many years providing Chinese/American dishes to the neighborhood at affordable prices.  Although there are two tables in the house, the lack of heat in winter makes it obvious they don't expect (want) people to consume their products there.  So, when I ordered sesame chicken and hot/sour soup and indicated I would eat while the food was at its peak heat, they asked me twice if they understood me correctly.

They did, and pulled out a plastic orange tray to deliver the take away containers to me, along with cheap utensils.  They were kind enough to remove the staples used to close the styro lid, so that I could gain prompt access.  

My lunch was pretty much okay.  

The hot & sour soup was made without MSG, and had a good taste with ample tofu and veggies, and the right amount of vinegar.  The sesame chicken was not over breaded, and the meat could be tasted, and was not lost in the goop.  The quantity was plenty for a midday meal.  The fried rice had been made earlier, had the tint of the bouillon it had been cooked in, and had a fairly fresh texture of being prepared earlier in the day, not yesterday.  

Overall, it was what was expected from this type of kitchen, and perhaps, slightly above average based on the soup and rice.  

The price/quality ratio was just about right, but having to wear a coat while eating is inhospitable, and knocks it down from average to just below.

This Dunkin Donuts on Bustleton Avenue in the far Northeast Philadelphia, is about average for this species of fried round dough outlets. Small footprint, but with a corner lounge with worn out leatherette sofa and easy chair, and slate accent wall. 

Nice touches, but it comes down to the quality of their bread and butter - their coffee and sweet dough. In this they cannot complete with the new wave of cafes, bakeries and donut specialty houses that are working harder for my dollar. In the last two weeks I have tasted far better java, and munched on way more luxurious cakes and dough fry around town and the burbs, than sampled last night. Maybe a little more money, but the difference in quality is patent. Too, they don't sweep the floor around you while sitting down to enjoy their wares. No one likes dust and dirt flying around their food. No one wants to feel swept out. 

DD. Too much of a no longer great thing. Becoming stale; much like day old donuts.

Crystal Diner (formerly Edgewater Queen) in Edgewater Park, NJ, is a small footprint roadside attraction on southbound Route 130. It looks recently renovated with stone and stainless fascade, and has a cozy if crowded ambiance. I sat down at the end of the counter and was immediately welcomed by a few of the staff hustling their platters and coffee pots. 

The menu was a tour de force of traditional diner cuisine with several pages just for breakfast. I went with something small (I thought) before a more elaborate and expensive meal. The breakfast sandwich (sausage, egg & cheese on kaiser) seemed about right. I asked my server if they used quality rolls as opposed to the poor varieties found in some kitchens. She assured me theirs were good. 

They weren't.

What arrived minutes later was a large plate, half of which was loaded with home fried potatoes, and a transected sandwich with long toothpicks holding the two halves together. I didn't mind that they used links rather than patties, even when they began to roll out of the sandwich. No biggie. However, the kaiser was a cheap imitation of an actual bakery product. It was crushed, lifeless and tasteless. What was worse were the home fries. They lacked flavor and were dry beyond redemption. Not even salt, pepper and hot sauce could salvage them. It was obvious that the kitchen didn't have a clue and that management was likely part of the conspiracy. 

When was the last time anyone sampled their offerings to provide quality control? Not often enough. 

It was a full house, so I expect I am whistling in the wind, but it is one and done for me.

Robert Morris, a signer of the Declaration of Independence, The Articles of Confederation and the Constitution, left his name to this old river burg, and even had his home, Summerseat, nearby. It was his plan to have the capital of the new United States established right here in Morrisville, PA. He was off target by about 25 miles, as the ultimate vote landed our first national city in Philadelphia. Still, Morris was nothing, if not ambitious for his adopted home town (He was born in England, and arrived here as a teenager). 

How would he feel about having a tavern named after him?  He would probably have enjoyed the notoriety of being associated with a dive bar with smoking privileges, but lacking a kitchen for a meal, and even taps for the beer they serve. Bottles and cans only, folks. Yet, he probably would have supped and indulged his muses elsewhere, as the joint has seen better days, and is now far from its prime.  The crowd is friendly, if loud and in its cups. The suds are priced right, and the barkeeps a smiling, tolerate group. 

My aluminum Bud Light (Philly Philly) edition, was $3. Hard to beat that coinage for a long cold one. 

Still, I couldn't escape the sensation that old Robert M., for all his wealth and colonial political power, would have only visited this establishment when he didn't want to be seen by anyone who would recognize him. It is easy to understand why.

This Giant on West Trenton Avenue in Morrisville is the same size as its sisters in Lower Makefield and Langhorne (Newtown), and has more or less the same inventory, but it does feel more dark and dingy than those other stores.  When I shop there, the lack of adequate lighting makes it a bit oppressive to spend much time.  The absence of the smaller, modern, carts available elsewhere, makes it necessary to use the larger, older and rustier pushers that often have gimpy wheels.  

While it wouldn't take much to upgrade this commercial space into a more pleasant facility, the company seems to have decided to leave it as it is.  Perhaps, their lease is coming to an end, or the revenue from this location does not justify the expenditure.  Regardless, aside from the convenience of stopping in here occasionally, I would avoid it and frequent the newer and easier to navigate markets just to the north for the same prices.

Read Whitney A. from Holland review (12/2/12), which mirrors my own. 
The staff is very friendly and fast, the price is reasonable, and the coffee decent. All good things. But, the bagels are not close to being the right texture nor taste. They could be so much better with a little tinkering.  It's not that they are bad, it's just that they miss the target of being really satisfying. 
With so many bagelphiles adrift at the loss of Bagel Junction, Newtown Bagel could become our Shangri-la, and garner our undying devotion and business with a few adjustments.

What Happened to the Copa brand?

Back in the Day, when Copabanana was only down on South Street, I spent my Friday nights after Tai Chi classes at the Painted Bride hanging out with the motley crew at Copa, downing rip roaring 'ritas, and munching fabulous Burgers laden with Pepper Jack Cheese and sliced Jalapenos, with a basket of Spanish Flies fulfilling a post workout greasy comfort food attack, and exchanging stories of daring do.  So very Yin/Yang. I either sat at the bar, in the dining room, or upstairs in the cramped attic before it became a cooler than you microbar. 

Cut to the recent past, and I finally had a couple of opportunities to hit this Copa on Spruce Street, just off Penn's Campus.  Looked great from the outside - loads of colors - and even suggested some happening things within. One stop at the bar for drinks and eats, and another at a small corner table, left me scratching my kep and wondering whether it was my faulty memory, or the joint's loss of verve, that left me feeling that I was in the wrong Copa.  

Yes.  The drinks were still stiff (one was enough for me), but the grub had fallen off a cliff.  My beloved burger memory suffered a rude awakening when I bit into what looked to be the same TexMex heat burger of ancient lore.  What had been a juicy joy had evolved into the proverbial hockey puck.  Hard from over-grilling, well done from inattention, and spiced by over-aged now gray peppers from absent quality control and pride.

 Not once, but on both occasions, I departed a saddened and wistful patron, yearning for the old days when a Copaburger meant joy on a bun.

TWO SLICE SPECIAL REVIEW ONLY

The price at $4.99 for two large slices of pizza and a soft drink was excellent.  The size of the slices was also more than expected. The service was friendly.  The room was small, with only two tables for those who want to eat their pizza just out of the oven when it is at its prime. So, this is basically a take out joint. 

We wanted a quick bite to tide us over until dinner. A slice apiece and sharing the drink was our intention. 

I requested that the reheat be "well done," in order to bring the ingredients back to life after sitting on display. 

What we received were slices that were not hot in the center where the cheese was thickest. That was likely due to the excessive amount of cheese piled onto the pie, out of proportion to the tomato sauce which seemed sparingly used. The result was pizza that could not be picked up by the crust because it was too heavy on the topside.  The taste was weak because of the cheese/sauce imbalance, and perhaps the quality of the cheese and sauce themselves.  The crust would have been improved with a little salt added to the dough.  

Not an impressive effort by Pizza Land.

F. W. Woolworth built a retail empire at the end of the 19th into the mid twentieth centuries, out of the "Five & Dime" store concept. In its heyday it had over 5,000 stores on 4 continents. One of those iconic enterprises was build on Haddon Avenue in downtown Collingswood, NJ. Today, the high tintype ceiling, wood plank floored space is where Sabrina's Cafe holds court. Walking in from the rear parking lot the room feels cavernous and a real blast from the past. 

It sounded that way, too. Without acoustic softening from all the cheap clothing Woolworths used to sell, the crash and clang of scraping chairs, dozens of conversations, kitchen noise and background music, made for very discordant uncomfortable ambience. If they hung tapestries rather than blackboards, and placed sound panels strategically along the ceiling, Sabrina's would be a much more pleasant restaurant to visit and hang out. As it is, regardless of food quality it is not welcoming enough to be worth a return.

What about my breakfast last week? Well, it left a lot to be desired. My server was pleasant and efficient, but never brought the milk requested with their good coffee. She probably couldn't hear me. Their signature Challah thick cut french toast looked great, but the egg/sugar/cinnamon mix had not penetrated into the body of the slices, making it dry and tough chewing. There was sweetness baked into the bread, but even melted butter and poured syrup did not significantly reduce its lack of moisture within. I took half home thinking I might be able to salvage it in my kitchen, but by the next morning it had lost all freshness and couldn't be revived. RIP. 

I wonder what good old Frank Winfield Woolworth would do about this situation? It was he and his brother Charles who added the lunch counters to their successful stores and made them a new part of American culture. They would no doubt figure out how to perfect the experience and make more money doing it right.

Although I'm sure they had something else in mind in naming this Chinese fast food establishment at the corner of Castor Avenue and Unruh Street in Northeast Philly, that " Boom" can signify the other side of explosive pleasurable cuisine, and be something quite the contrary. Unfortunately, that was where our experience cratered. 

We stopped in for late lunch around 3 when part of the menu shifted from lunch to dinner prices. As all ordering is done online even when sitting in the restaurant, it made for some confusion in both ordering and paying. To make matters worse, there were two menus - a paper menu on the tables and a very different online ordering menu, that were not well coordinated. 

So, while we wanted and thought we ordered beef soup with dumplings; what we got was just poorly crafted dumplings with thick skin and low flavor. Disappointing. Beyond that, the Vietnamese style spring rolls @$3.95 for twins, was mostly cabbage within. Double whammy!  Finally, the beef sandwich was basically a soft scallion pancake rolled up with "meat" inside and a squirt of hoisin sauce for sweetener. While the best of the bunch, it left alot to be desired. 

No doubt this Boom Buns is primarily a takeout joint, and customers are far away when they open the bag and see what they got (BOOM!) For those of us eating in house, the sound of deflated expectations created a rumbling crash in our stomachs (BOOM)! 

Maybe the Xao Long Bao is the way to go here, but we'll never know, because a return visit is just not in the cards. There is too much competition in this growing Asian neighborhood for anyone to give Boom Buns a second try. 

DOUBLE BOOM!!

Of the limited Chinese options in the Newtown area, this place is by far the worst. 
Strictly take out unless you want to sit at one of the two odd sized tables covered with newspapers. 
Several Guangzhou brothers operate this relocated tiny shop.  The kitchen is in full view, and it is not always pleasant to watch how the food prep is done. 
As someone else suggested, this is a place to go only when all the alternatives are blown away by a storm.

Standard Dunkin outlet, perhaps in need of some TLC to spruce it up. My evening stop for a jolt of joe and sweet round dough found  their front doors in need of hydraulic repair to keep them from crashing back behind me, and in need of a sweeping. 

Service was fine. The coffee decent. The donuts forgettable. 

Just back from Southern California where independent donut shops abound. I wonder why that niche market hasn't taken off here? That competition would be great and raise the donut bar to new creative sugary heights.

Asian Taste Inn in the Huntingdon Valley Marketplace on County Line Road, is a primarily Chinese house owned by a Guangdong Province family, that has been turning out pretty good semi-authentic dishes for a while.  The space is well maintained with many booths and tables, and an amiable server corps dressed in tan and green that actually seems to enjoy interacting with their customers.  

True to its cultural roots, the cuisine tends toward sweetness, and even their spicy dishes maintain a hint of sugar just behind the chili flavors.  Our Orange Beef and General Tso Shrimp came either drowned in heavy sweet amber, or had it on the side.  Both were framed in Broccoli Florets, the much overused non-Chinese veggie. Their tastes were fine, but we all commented on the unexpected sugariness of the platters.  The Spicy Shrimp, Scallop & Squid with Pepper Corn Salt, was a relief from the cane, and would have been completely on target had it all been crisper.  Finally, my sushi sample of an Eel & Avocado Roll was average, with much more Avo than Eel, and artificially colored Wasabe and Ginger.  

Bottom Line - The suburbs has taken the edge off the kitchen here.  Everything was accommodating to the local market.  Too much broccoli, and not enough real heat. Not bad if this is what you are looking for.

Came down to 40th Street to meet a good friend, and parked right in front of Tandoor India.  When he arrived, I asked where he wanted to go, and he pointed to the doorway right behind me.  Auspicious beginnings...
First impression was of an old establishment somewhat in need of refurbishment, but with inviting scents of curry and coriander drawing us in.  I checked the buffet as we walked past to our table and saw an extensive collection of yellow, red, brown and rusty sauces, all looking fresh and inviting on a cold Sunday night.  The place was not crowded.  Settling in, I decided to take a look at the menu because I was not in the mood for a cascade of flavors and tastes, but wanted to relax with only a few.  We were given copies of the take out menu, which somewhat surprised me.  On the cover it said: "We believe that the joy of eating lies in the art of fine cooking."
I'll drink to that.
We ordered Tikka Masala (with Chicken), which came out in a fine pink sauce of tomato and ginger, and was quite good. The Baigan Bharta was tasty, but was chopped fine rather than with the chunky eggplant I expected.  They cheated a bit on the Garlic Naan by bringing us regular Naan painted with garlic butter.  It didn't work, as it was not integrated into the bread, but sat on the surface, and lacked the baked garlic pieces I love in true Garlic Naan.  A disappointing way to pay an extra buck. The Mango Lassi was pretty good,  but a little thin from using milk rather than yogurt.  A nice plate of rice came with the meal.  
This was a meal in which we were more engrossed in the conversation than attentive to our food.  The strong brotherhood carried the day, and the meal became background.  For the overall experience, I was quite satisfied.
We didn't solve any world problems, but agreed we would get together soon, and try again.

Tough crowd!

Coffee depends on the quality of the water.  Here, you might want to have it tested. Definitely has an unusual aftertaste.  Still, it was potable and left no lingering aftereffects.  

Can't speak to the sweets, but the bathroom was tidy.

While the Shops At Liberty Place offer an architecturally interesting structure in a modern urban environment, and attracts people for both shopping and sightseeing the latest in city planning, it also likely represents a business model that will not succeed in the long run.  

The suburban mall made its presence felt as a post World War II phenomenon that mirrored the rapid growth of the automobile industry and the closely aligned migration of a generation of city dwellers into the countryside, a/k/a Suburbia.  They were the successful way to provide the "stuff" of life away from the urban core.  They worked well for almost 50 years.  But, as with most things, they were overdone, and failed to adapt to the changing demographics and cultural evolution that they spawned.  Walk through most malls today and you see lots of empty space, failing stores, and a subculture of youth versus elderly hangouts.  

First the malls disrupted Main Street.  Then the Walmarts and Costco's of the world, disrupted the malls.  But, the disassociation from the communities where the consumer lived ultimately started to alienate them.  People wanted to return to their Main Street where possible.  More began to appreciate the quality of city life, and returned to the urban centers to once again live and work in the same place.  The suburbs began to lose its charm for many, especially those without young children.  

These reurbanified folk did not want to shop in malls along an inhuman highway, and certainly did not want to spend much time in a suburban style mall transplanted in the city.  The developers who thought otherwise, are wishing they had been smarter.  The retail franchisers and chain expanders were the last to catch on, but the growing list of failing stores and malls bear witness to this truth.  

So it is with the Shops of Freedom Place.  Fundamentally, a suburban marketplace miscast as a modern upscale urban experience that it turned out not enough people really wanted.  A J. Crew in a Center City suburban style mall just does not attract enough customers.  Never will. 

It is not that such a public space could never work.  It can, but it requires a total reconfiguration that demonstrates an understanding of what people really want.  What is that?  A return to the village life, or that of the old neighborhood, where people knew each other, and felt like part of a community - in the city.  More impersonal and monotonous shopping is not where we are headed.  

How accomplish that?  Start by thinking in human scale.  Change part of the Liberty Place skyscrapers into condos and apartments for people to live.  Add a supermarket, cinema, child care, medical facility, and more greenery throughout the buildings.  Create a vertical village or neighborhood.  Where are the green grocer, the deli, the bakery, the corner tavern? 

The central rotunda can still work as a gathering place for activities, but it should feel more like the gazebo in the middle of the public commons.  

People want their cities to be state of the art, cutting edge, and full of energy and opportunity.  But, they also want to feel like it can take care of their needs and make them feel part of it, not overcome by it.  There are examples of this being done successful around the country and the planet.  Visit some of the new cities in Asia, and even some of the new age projects in New York, Seattle(JB) and San Francisco.  

Bring it down to human scale, and they will come and thrive.

I am just getting into BBQ in a bigger way, so when I saw Christopher D's review of Oink Johnson's Southern BBQ along with the few others, I had a strong impulse to drive up county and find out for myself what this place had to offer. It was a gorgeous early September afternoon special made for a open window stereo blazing cruise in the rolling Bucks countryside. I was in a good mood.

Driving up 611 north of Doylestown with the GPS alerting me that I was at my destination, I still did not recognize it at first.  There is a small cabin on wheels sitting in the middle of the rocky parking lot, with a fruit stand on one side, and a puppy barn on the other.  That trailered shack was Oink's.  The front porch of the structure has two large BBQ grills, a large menu nailed to the wall.  Took a few seconds to get oriented, especially when this big fella with a white apron and big white mustache came over and looked down at me and said:

"What'll it be, young feller?"

"Well, sir. I can't decide 'tween the Pulled Pork and the Brisket. What do ya think?"

"They're both lip smackin' good, my man.  Can't go wrong with either." 

Ok. I was hooked by ol' Oink's charm even before I made a choice.  This guy and the whole set up was right out of a Michener novel.  I was game to play my role. 

Two of his buddies sat to the side of the shack under an old beer company umbrella watching this transaction.  I looked over to greet them with a reference to the weather, and they chawed back that maybe I should get one of both the pork and brisket. Nice upsell, gents. 

I ordered the Pulled Pork Sandwich, BBQ Beans and Corn Bread.  Oink disappeared into the enclosed portion of the hut on wheels to make his magic.  He appeared a few minutes later with a large white paper wrapped package that seemed too big to be a Sammy.  I couldn't see what was in it, which was just slightly troubling, but this man had such an aura of confidence that I let it slide thinking I was probably missing the point of just knowing it would be great without a need for a visual. 

This place is strictly take out, so although I would have preferred to enjoy my BBQ on site, I had to take with and drive back home to eat it.  No biggie.

Upon unwrapping the creation I found it was indeed a huge quantity of meat, but the roll had been saturated with pork and BBQ juices, and was too wet to eat. I ate the pork with a fork.  It was tender and juicy, yet the BBQ flavor was not very strong, and it was a bit salty for my palate. The Beans were richly dark brown, heavy with molasses and chunks of fat back bacon. Excellent. The Corn Bread in the form of a muffin was good, but not overly sweet nor moist. 

If I could give a grade just for personality and appearance, Oink Johnson would be a 5 Star experience. But, as the Pulled Pork was not as good as others I have eaten, and the roll was a total loss, the food comes in at 2 Stars for me.

I will get back there eventually to try the ribs and brisket, but I am disappointed by the lack of "Zing" in the Pulled Pork.

Still, I recommend stopping in as the characters are wonderful, the locale very pretty farmland, and the food worth a sampling.

I found myself hungry around noon in Doylestown today, and decided to check out Hickory Kitchen for an early lunch. 

First impression was that this was an efficient, sunny, Main Street bistrot serving everything from soups to burgers to BBQ, with a large vegetarian option.  I almost went for the Special Bison Burger after having just had a Yelp discussion about buffalo burgers, but had eaten enough meat yesterday, and just didn't want more.  So, I went for the Grilled Veggie Quesadilla and home brewed Sweet Peach Iced Tea.  The chef and server got busy at the grill, and produced my meal in about 10 minutes. It came out on a small aluminum baking tray (clever), with Sour Cream, Salsa, and a bag of chips (?). 

The Quesadilla was very good, and I could not finish it. It was full of chunky veggies and cheese.  The Iced Tea was fine, just lightly sweetened. Each table had three bottle rockets with three varieties of BBQ sauce - mustard, maple, and tomato based. I tried each of them on the quesadilla in place of the jar based salsa.  I liked them more than the salsa, and think HK is onto something as an alternative to the traditional accompaniment for Mexican dishes.  The mix of Mexi - BBQ could be a big hit (but, it is not Tex-Mex).

This review will likely be updated when I return to taste the BBQ options here. Most of the raves seem to be for the ribs, so I will get back for them. 

All in all, a good first bite, but I can't say that I am drawn enough to return promptly that being a fan suggests.  A nice effort with potential.

Kelly's Kitchen is the actual name of this breakfast/lunch café sitting at the bottom of Bristol Road in Bensalem.  It has a nice counter with about a dozen spinners, and an equal number of tables, but the kitchen is in the back of the house so you can't see the meals being prepared, nor smell of the bacon on the grill. 

The service is good with prompt offers of coffee refills and light banter to make you feel at home.  My Kelly's Irish Omelet was a three egger with Onions, Peppers and Cheddar alongside a huge pile of crispy Home Fries, and Rye Toast.  I thought the eggs could have been lighter in texture if mixed with a little water before cooking, and there wasn't a whole lot of the veggies inside the eggs.  It was a bit underwhelming for a House Special.  The potatoes and toast were both fine.

The absence of credit card acceptance is annoying in today's world, and retailers who choose not to make their customer's lives easier in this regard should be called to account.  

While the room and service were fine, the food was not consistently exceptional, and the Cash Only policy shows a lack of true concern for its customers. Hard to get past A-OK.

Comfortable Star$$$ in the Acme Shopping Center just south of Bordentown off Route 130.  

Not a fan of their burnt approach to java, but sometimes it is the only option in the vicinity.  The Flat White was fine, but the prices are designed to make the stockholders happier than the customers.  

This shop was well laid out with ample table and comfortable seating around.  No problem with the staff.  Everyone was in a good mood this mid-week late morning.  Several quiet conversations and solitary students around and about.

Grand Opening of Chinese take out joint on South Broad Street, Trenton.  

It has a postage stamp size dining area with only 2 tables for eating in, and 3 chairs for waiting on take away.  The space is still clean and the kitchen shiny, as it has been open little more than a week.  

The menu is extensive and basically a traditional Chinese/American emporium.  Nothing authentic, but if you wanted really good Chinois you would not be parking your wheels on S. Broad in the first place.  My Orange Flavored Chicken was a load in the styro container they give to even those who eat in.  The chicken was fresh enough, and had not been deeply frozen.  The sauce was gloopy orange colored, although the taste of the citrus was weak, despite the orange peel in the mix.  The Fried Rice was a bright yellow from the dye used in the bullion stock that morning.  It had plenty of roast pork and veggies in it, but I did not see much (if any) egg scrambled into it.  

The people here are Fuzhounese, the province just north of old Canton, and across the straits from Taiwan.  Their cuisine is similar to Cantonese, but has some other influences.  It tends toward less sweetness, but close enough to allow for success in the Chinese take out wars.  

If you are interested, go soon while everything is new and clean.  The owners are there and take an interest in getting things right.  Just remember what you are dealing with, and you will not be disappointed.

PRO TIP - They don't serve hot tea!

Solid Chinese/American house in Lalor Plaza. 20 years at this nearly invisible location. Owners are friendly and hard working.  The shop could be cleaner and the supplies stored out of sight, but the grub is reliable, if not exceptional.  
While it will not become a standby option, it is worth remembering it is there for that time when the yen for Egg Foo Young or Sweet & Sour Pork overcomes you.

Some specifics - My Wonton Soup with the lunch combo was low average.  While the broth was standard, the wontons had exceptionally thick skin which detracted from the overall enjoyment of the bowl.  The Egg Foo Young was better, with fresh veggies and a decent brown sauce.  I don't know if they make their own wontons, but these had a very familiar feel to them, suggesting mass production from an outside vendor.  

While a dive, once accepted as such, the experience was fine.

I don't know why this Rite Aid was so difficult to find on Yelp*, but it finally showed up.

Drug stores today have morphed from the corner mom and pop shop into a semi - big box convenience store that also sells prescription medications along with food, drink, and photo services.  It must be working as these modern day behemoths are spreading like a bad cold (poor pun).  

This one does a decent job getting my prescriptions out quickly, and the drive thru option is a nice touch for those unable to park a car or walk into the store.  The crew is friendly and helpful.  Too, I have been known to pick up a chocolate bar in the candy isle, and a birthday card in the excessively large greeting card isle.  

I bow to modernity, although I miss the personal touch of the old fashioned Rexall (now a cool Starbucks here in Newtown).

Apple Cleaners is located in Goodnoe Corner on Sycamore Street, Newtown.  In a previous incarnation an office supply store occupied this space very close to The Green Parrot. 
I don't claim any special expertise when it comes to professional cleaners.  I just want my shirts and pants done well and ready when I come to claim them.  Apple has been keeping me satisfied for the time they have been here.  The customer service is friendly, and they can remove spots that are pointed out to them. 
Oh, and they seldom return my dress shirts with broken buttons; one of my serious peeves. 
I offer three stars because although I am quite happy with Apple, I am not sure that being a "Fan" or having an orgasm (Woohoo!) really expresses the more moderate emotional response I have to a clean shirt.

Empress Garden is a small shop on N. 10th Street in Chinatown, Philly, that changed hands about a year ago.  The original owner (the "Empress"), was a sterling hostess and stunning beauty who ran her house efficiently and with admirable warmth.  The food had a Taiwanese and Indonesian orientation, but also had the standard American/Chinese dishes for those who preferred them.  Their fruit drinks were freshly squeezed, and it had a strong following. 

I returned after an absence of a few years, and my first run with the new operation.  While the menu was basically the same as before, the actual plates coming from the kitchen seemed to have lost a bit of their edge.  We ordered Scallion Pancakes, Curry Chicken with Onions, Salt & Pepper Pork Chops, Orange Beef and Sautéed String Beans.  A lot for the three of us to consume, but we were looking forward to bring the balance home.  

While the Scallion Pancakes were good, they are certainly returned to the norm, and were not as exceptional as remembered.  The Chicken dish had the right taste and fresh chicken, but the Onions were harder than desired, and thus tended to dominate the dish.  The S & P Pork Chops had been a wonderful platter in the past, but this day the breading and meat was over-deep fried, making it tougher in the bite, and less enjoyable in the chew.  Disappointing.  The Orange Beef was the best thing on our table, with a nice spicy, not overly gloopy, sauce.  It was fun to eat even with the orange peel in its soft non-burnt condition.  Finally, the Veggies were fine with a light Garlic finish.  

The meal was satisfactory, but not what I hoped for based on recollection.  Empress Garden was now just another Chinatown restaurant with a fair kitchen and price, but nothing to make it outstanding.

232 Corner Café (formerly Hogeland's) is a pleasant surprise. 

When the former luncheonette closed last year due to the landlord's expectation that this space would be taken over by a medical provider outpatient clinic at substantially higher rents, those of us who knew and loved the old gal were sad and disappointed.  It appeared to be the end of an iconic local institution that had been around, while changing hands, for nearly half a century.  Progress to some.  Loss of culture to others. 

The "best laid plans...sometimes go astray...", and when the plans for the medical facility shrunk to a smaller piece of the strip mall, this corner was not included.  All the fixtures remained intact, and a new business bloomed out of the ashes of the old. Ron now runs the operation, and at first blush, the new order of things feels much like the former enterprise.  The counter and tables are the same.  The grill and coffee brew where they sat before.  The menu has been updated, but the kitchen still puts out very good breakfasts (and lunches).  

My French Toast was done right.  The standard two slices were dipped in an egg/vanilla/cinnamon mix, and grilled expertly with caramelized edges.  The taste was what I wanted, and I appreciated that the "small stack" was now the main size for the plate.  A melt of butter; and splash of syrup, and I was a happy man.  The New England Roast Bunn drip java was hot, fresh and repeatedly refilled by Ron as he entertained the troops.  

232 Corner Café is a victory for the community.  Come on down and join in the celebration.

UPDATE - JULY 13, 2018: There are signs of change since the last time I was here for breakfast in 2016. They now use a generic food purveyor coffee rather than New England beans. Too, the quality of their Kaiser roll has declined to a soft unibread that lacks a crusty texture and is basically white bread stamped into the form of a roll. 
Considering a downgrade to 3 stars.

Thirty years ago when I first moved to Bucks County from Trenton, Aldo's was only All Star Pizza in the Village Shires Shopping Center.  A generation later it has expanded into a nice size full fledged Italian restaurant named after its founder.  This all happened gradually, and it seemed to reflect the overall growth of this area. Farms began to grow suburban housing developments. Those new folks needed local places to eat. Etc. The dinners were good, and we could walk there from home.  

Stopped in for lunch the other day with my bud, Phil.  I guess I was in a rediscovery mood, as I had just visited Not Just Wings in the same center the weekend before.  We opted for a couple of plain slices for Phil, and an Eggplant Parmiagana Sandwich on a torpedo roll for me.  

Phil knows from pizza (tomato pie) as he is from the Burg in Trenton.  I watched him hold each slice up to test their rigidity, and satisfied, devour them.  He smiled and said they were very good, but not like Papa used to make, or even his uncles DeLorenzo. 

 The Parm was large, crusty and sealed in melted Mozza.  It, too, was decent, especially the toasted roll which was a joy to eat.  The Eggplant itself was cut into long, thick pieces, and were still a bit firm to the bite.  I prefer them to be completely soft from being sautéed in light breading and olive oil before being torched in the pizza oven.  The Sauce was ok, but lacked a distinctive flavor.  I go for Eggplant Parm Sandys often, and this one passed the acceptable test, but did not stand out.  I would not rush back to have it again.  

I may return for dinner in the near future, as they still evoke fond memories.  When I do, I will update this review.  But, for now, Aldo's for lunch is simply Okay. However, I may take a cue from Phil and stick with slices.

This is a franchised large format Japanese Hibachi house that also offers sushi and a few "fusion" offerings from China and Thailand.  This style restaurant seems to be coming into fashion on the East Coast, although it is more played out on the Left Coast. 

This one is apparently under new management, and they are attempting to make the facility more comfortable and attractive.  They have done a good job on the creature comforts, and the service is also attentive, except for the minor language difficulties in understanding each other through the Korean and South Jerzee accents.  

I was the guest this night, and my hostess did all the ordering.  I opted for the sushi side of the joint, although the Hibachi room was more active and colorful, especially when they performed their volcano show with the ball of fire shooting into the air.  Luckily, we could see that from the safe distance on the far side of the room.  

The Clear Soup was quite good as part of the dinner package.  The Sashimi platter (Deluxe?) was ample with a nice variety of well sliced fresh fish.  They all had good taste, but I would have preferred them slightly cooler.  I tasted all the offerings, but was not feeling compelled to finish them.  The Rolls (Sorry. The names were not disclosed to me) were okay, but not exciting.  Typical sushi rolls, but why the chef put cream cheese in it is beyond me.  Do they even have that in Japan?  This is not something I would consider ordering on my own.  Maybe this is what is popular in this part of South Jersey, or because it is close to Philly, cream cheese is a concession to local culture. Fish and cream cheese? No. Thank you!

I was happy to have dinner with a friend, and content to let her treat in return for something I handled for her.  Still, something more authentically Japanese would tempt me more than this Korean version of an Americanized Japanese Hibachi/Sushi store.  It just didn't hang together for me.

Miami Beach has its Big Pink diner-esque food forum. Furlong has its Back to the 50's; a pink edifice loaded with nostalgia for days gone by when the Victrola and AM radio were the only ways to listen to contemporary music.  This place is replete with black and whites of Elvis and Marilyn, and the lesser lights of the mid-20th Century.

It is a breakfast/lunch emporium with a dozen or so booths and the same number of tables.  The coffee comes fast and furious, delivered by black clad waitresses calling everybody, "honey," "doll," or "sugarcakes."  Ya' gotta' luv it!

The breakfasts are pretty good, with many fresh fruit specials added to pancakes, waffles and French toast. Still, nothing that makes me want to rush back for more. 

Yu wan meat wid dat?

Big Q BBQ sits out in front of H Mart and looks like a weird Sonic Drive In. 

I've only sampled their wares once; buying a St. Louis Ribs dinner and Fried Chicken platter with sides of Chak & Meez and Baked Beans with Ends.  Waiting in the antechamber felt a bit odd because while there were plenty of people in gray shirts in the kitchen, I did not see anyone working with the food.  Too, as someone else mentioned, there was no odor of smoked meats, nor BBQ sauces, nor even of frying chicken.  It was almost as if the food was prepared elsewhere and shipped here for sale.  No smoker outside, either. 

The food is really just okay. The Chicken was the better of the main offerings.  The breasts were large and juicy, although the breading would have shone off with more spice.  The Ribs were dense and coated in a thick ruddy sauce, but it seemed that there was insufficient liquidity to really impact the meat.  It made for a dry texture with underwhelming flavor.  Knife and fork were helpful in separating meat from bone, and when gnawing at them with dirty fingers they were not particularly tender, but good enough to be worth the effort.  I prefer a looser presentation with more gravy, but that is a matter of taste.  

The sides were actually pretty good.  The Mac & Cheese was pretty much standard creamy fare, but the Beans were surprisingly hearty and well spiced.  

No rush to go back to Big Q, as there are better fried chicken places close by, and while a bit of up country driving is needed to find more authentic homespun Q, I would sooner cruise the countryside in search of that holy grail (or rack).

TJ Smith's on Easton Road near the border between Doylestown and Warrington gives the feel of a western mountain lodge - all exposed wood and stone, high vaulted ceilings and beams.  The bar room where we ate was spacious on a weekday afternoon, and the service was friendly and informative.  

We opted for their 4 beer sampler to go with their self-proclaimed famous burgers and a cheesesteak.  At $8.50 for the 3 oz. glasses, the price was about right, and the offerings of national brew was tasty and interesting, although 2 of them had a pumpkin component in honor of the season.  They were fine.  

The burgers were large (8 oz.) with the appropriate fixings, although both of them came out beyond the medium finish requested, which, with an empty house was hard to understand other than inattentiveness at the grill. Their tastes were good, and the beef had not been frozen.  The cheesesteak was average and clearly not their forte. 

Plenty of HDTVs everywhere for those who want sports stimulation while eating or drinking (this is a sports bar), but not so overwhelming as to be a distraction to conversation.  

Attractive house.  With more attention to detail, it could be an exceptional stop in an otherwise nondescript strip of Bucks County.

A convenient Star$$$$ for this part of the world, with access from both Street Road and Second Street Pike.  Its proximity to some of my favorite restaurants - Aroi Thai, Blue Sage and House of Pho - make it a perfect quick après dinner stop for hot brew on the way to the movies or home.  

It is not the most attractive franchise unit in the area, but it serves a functional purpose. 

Unlike a box of chocolates, you always know what you are going to get.

Returned today for lunch at 12:30.  

The small dining area was crowded, but I found a deuce in the corner nearest the work area and settled in after ordering their Apple Sausage Special.  

It arrived about 10 minutes later, a small, but tasty Apple Pork Sausage with Maple Chipotle BBQ Sauce, Grilled Onions, and a boatload of fries.  While it was a very good lunch, a couple of observations need be made.  First, the roll of a potato hot dog roll, which was not as good as a crusty French or Italian alternative would have been.  Second, there were a lot more fries than sausage.  They were good fries, but made the sandwich seem even smaller by comparison. 

Still, I liked the ambiance, service, and overall brightness of the place, and did not mind that they made some presentation decisions that detracted from what could have been an exceptional lunch.  

Certainly worth many returns.

Rolling in from Westmoreland County on the Pa Pike, my stomach started growling after almost four hours on the road.  I was near exit 312.  I pulled out my trusty sidekick Mobile Yelp and dialed in "Thai Restaurant."  It came back with two choices in the vicinity, so I opted for the one nearer my location.

Thai Place has an unassuming name, but under its self deprecating identity lurks a very fine Thai kitchen and comfortable dining space turning out very good authentic grub. Where many other restos of this genre approach the atmospherics with dark wood and musty scents, this shop is bright, light, and airy.  The owner works the front of the house enthusiastically, while the single server on the floor managed a warm smile and genuine concern for all the patrons. 

I ordered the Tom Yum Soup (Vegetables) and Drunken Noodles (Chicken).  Both were excellent.  They asked my preferred spice level between 1 and 3, and I asked for max spice.  That's the way I got it, right at the point where my sinuses start to run. Love it!  There were plenty of Veggies and Tofu in the soup, and even more in the Drunken Noodles.  There was enough for dinner the next night.  

The only reason Thai Place did not reach the apex was that my Jasmine Tea arrived in a lovely lime green mug with a teabag, rather than a pot of brewing boiling water and loose tea leaves.  That is the best way to achieve full bodied flavor, and requires fewer return visits to refill the mug with hot water.  I get that good tea is expensive and often unappreciated, but for me it sets apart the very good from the superlative.

Mandarin Garden in Willow Grove, Pa., is a throwback type of Chinese restaurant, the kind I went to with family as a kid in New York. Larger space.  Silk wall hangings. Jade sculptures.  Large menu covering most things from Cantonese through Hunan and Szechuan delicacies.  Seniors taking advantage of the Early Bird specials.  My nostalgia surprised me. 

Most important, the food was very good.  We were celebrating a first birthday in the USA (Chinese national), and were hoping for something a little extraordinary.  Judging from the approving smiles as each dish was devoured, we got what we came for.  

Hot Green Tea arrived immediately along with the dry crisp noodles duck sauce and hot mustard so ubiquitous in Chinese/American houses.  I don't indulge in this table snack, but my friends did in large quantities.  I was selected to do all the ordering, and came up with the following choices: DanDan Noodles (Spicy), Gunpowder Chicken (moderate spice), Jumbo Walnut Shrimp (mild spicy), Crispy Beef with House Made Toffee Cashews (mild spice), Cumin Lamb (spicy), and Tsingtao Beer for all the birthday toasts throughout dinner.  

Realizing that management was Fuzhounese, we did not have high expectations in the spice department.  Their cuisine tends toward sweetness, but there was no harm in asking for some heat.  The kitchen handled each dish in their own fashion.  

The DanDan Noodles were topped with ground pork and a chili sauce mix that was warm, but not what I was hoping for.  Still, our server anticipated this and had given the table a small dish of chili sauce to upgrade the burn.  I used some of it, but my guests did not.  They were content with what was presented, and not as accustomed to heavy spice as me (Good to know).  

The Gunpowder Chicken was also on the mildly sweet side, with a trace of chili on the bird breading, but with the sauce sweetened by an apple.  Unusual, and enjoyable, even if not packing heat.  

The Cumin Lamb was the strongest dish, with plenty of tender meat and cumin, that brought a light sweat to the upper lip.  Not the killer dose of cumin piled on lamb chops in some shops, but strong enough to know they were trying to appease us.  

The Crispy Beef with Toffee Cashews, was also tending toward sweetness, but they had candied the nuts very well, and when eaten with the copious slices of lightly crisped beef, was fun to eat.  

Finally, the Jumbo Shrimp with Walnuts reinforced the theme that the house interpretation of spice and heat began from the perspective that food from this part of China was always degrees of sweetness or sourness, but not really chili pepper fire breathing dragons.  

Again, my friends were fine with all of this and genuinely enjoyed their meals.  It was my own blinders about Szechuan flames that was the issue, not the kitchen attempt to move their dial in my direction.  Once I realized that I was making myself too critical of the platters because I wanted my friends to be happy; and that they were already there and praising me for finding such a nice place to celebrate, that I was able to let go, and just roll with the food, and accept that it was really very good.  

Good lesson to learn.  Better to let the house do what it does well, than to ask them to conform to my unrealistic expectations.

As a facility to hold a large luncheon meeting for about 150 lawyers, this Wyndham Garden Hotel in the heart of Trenton, NJ, is reasonably decent. Walking distance from the courthouses, and parking deck next door, it is easily accessible for most who want to attend to get a good meal while listening to a quality presentation on the latest issues in internet discovery requirements and security. These Bench Bar lunches are always a good place to catch up with friends and hobnob with the judges in this vicinage. 

The banquet room was large enough to commodate all of us, had an adequate sound system that everyone could hear clearly, and a catering kitchen that put out a Cornish hen plate that was tasty and attractive. The carrot cake dessert was a bit over the top, but no one was complaining about the buttercream icing. 

Service was unabtrusive, but kept the meal moving and the water glasses full. 

Can't speak to the rooms above, but this operation handled our bar association meeting quite well.

Despite the hour long wait on Friday night, J.B. Dawson's in the Flowers Mill Shopping Center was worth the wait.  Normally, I would see the waiting room crowd and listen to the hostess's lament of the wait time, and walk out immediately. For some reason, my intuition counseled patience, so I took the radio buzzer they handed me, and found three seats to settle in.  

The  bar was packed with Friday Happy Hour folk getting their zip on, and the two HDTVs in the waiting area were soundlessly tuned to Disney Channel and ESPN.  No one seemed to be paying attention, and the peeps around me were all conversing or buried in their smartphones. The time passed quickly, and we were eventually led to a corner booth in the barroom.  Our server introduced herself, took drink orders and came back promptly to take our order.  We wanted to share the Baby Back Rib and Chicken Tender plate, while young man went with his standard Cheeseburger and Fries.  

Dinner took a little while due to the packed house, but not so long as to become an issue.  When it arrived in the hands of a different server, we beheld a half rack of Baby Backs nicely browned and caramelized on top, and a larger pile of Tempura coated white meat Chicken, plus sides of Garlic Mashed Potatoes and Spiced Apples.  I began to salivate involuntarily as the aroma of the BBQ sauce hit me.  I hoped the first bite would be as seductive.  

It was more than that.   

The meat easily pulled from the bone.  The taste was very good, and the texture just chewy and tender enough to be completely satisfying.  Although there was very little meat left on the bones, I found myself sucking on them to capture every last bit of BBQ taste.  If anything, the Chicken Tenders were even better and a much bigger surprise.  They were big strips of never frozen chicken, breaded in a Tempura style, that were juicy, lightly crunchy and delicious.  The small mound of Mashed Taters were a nice complement to the more exciting pig and bird, but did a great job absorbing whatever sauce was stuck to the plate.  The Spiced Apple was yet another change of directly with its tartness and heat.  

I did not see a smoker on the premises, nor smell it at work, but regardless of how the meal was prepared, the execution was high end and the experience very solidly worth a return visit.

Just returned to Keystone to buy 4 new tires. They recommended Continentals, and I agreed with their assessment of their quality and ride. 

On the way home, one of them blew out!  What?!  True.

I called and returned the next day for a replacement (They had to order it).  They apologized for the experience, although it was clearly a manufacturer's defect, and discounted it down to the cost of mounting and balancing (normally part of the quoted price). They handled the paperwork. 

While this was not a fun time, but Keystone stood behind the product and satisfied me of their integrity. I did not have to ask for some consideration. They offered it straight up. 

I did not mind the small cost of mounting the new tire in light of how well they handled the situation. 

5 Stars if they had taken care of all of it.

When you're down in Bensalem around Neshaminy Mall, finding a good Chinese/Sushi restaurant can be a challenge.  The AMC 24 is a nice place to watch a movie, but the "dinner and" part of that is limited in the immediate vicinity unless you like highway-style fast/casual food.  

Then there is Misto Diner, which I found courtesy of Yelp. As other reviewers said, the location on this site is off by about a mile.  It is further down Neshaminy Blvd after passing Bristol Road if coming from the rear of NM, in a small strip mall anchored by 7-11.  Keep going.  You will get there. It is worth the search, as the quality of the room and cuisine are considerably above the standard Chinese American shop.  

White table clothes and red cloth napkins are a nice touch suggesting a bit of quality control in the product.  The owner family is present and in charge.  They bring care and pride to the effort.  Although I did not ask, our server seemed to be the father.  He had a Jackie Chan appearance; friendly, engaged, and humorous.  His bifocals tried to hide his bemused visage as we asked questions about the menu and the history of the joint.  

We settled on Hot and Sour Soup, Chicken Broccoli in Garlic Sauce, and Shredded Pork Mei Fun.  The soup was a rich, thick, spicy mix.  We added a spoonful of Chili Oil to bring out more of the hot richness.  It was a nice improvement to an already good bowl of soup.  The Chicken dish was off menu as we asked for garlic sauce as opposed to the Hunan style base.  The meat was tender and very tasty.  The broccoli cut into small enough sprigs and excellently cooked.  The mei fun was also good, but not at the same level as the other dishes.

To be clear, Misto Diner is still a traditional Chinese American restaurant found in most suburban areas, but it is a very good one.  It should not be mistaken for an authentic Chinese restaurant found in more heavily Chinese populated parts of the region. But, if you find yourself in this neck of the woods this is a very good choice.  Too, they have no problem giving you an extra pot of tea if you want to wait there for your movie time.

It's a bit surprising to find a decent BBQ joint in a back room of the Best Western Motel on Street Road, Bensalem, Pa.  The place has almost zero atmosphere, no aroma of smoking meat, no beer spillage on the floor, and no one in boots nor large apron cutting the brisket.  There is only Julie, the matron of the house and jack of all serving trades, handling just about everything.  She bartends, takes food orders, serves everything that comes out of the kitchen, and then collects payment at the end of the night.  She makes it personal by asking everyone's first name, and remembering them throughout. 

Don't let the environment deter you from coming in.  The grub is very good.  First, there are several beers on tap or bottles, although on this Sunday night they seemed to be out of most of the good crafties.  Still, my End of The World draft was pleasantly cold and refreshing at $4 for 10oz. Friends seemed to be downing Yards brew as quickly as it was poured.  

My crew of three ordered Half BBQ Chicken (3 sides, corn bread, fries); Coffee Rubbed Brisket (3 sides, hush puppies, fries); and a third rack of St. Louis style Ribs (4 bones, 2 sides, fries).  There was a ton and a half of food.  And, it was all very good to amazing.  The Half Chicken came our golden skinned without a crack in the covering.  It was uber-moist and had a wonderful flavor.  It needed no accompanying sauce to kick it up a notch, as it was really an apex bird.  The Ribs were very good, but not the meatiest I have encountered.  The dry rub was very solid, but I found it needed a little liquid zing to get to my preferred taste level.  The table had 2 unmarked bottle rockets, one based in vinegar, the other, tomato.  Both okay, but not the strength of the cuisine.  

The unexpected star of the show was the Brisket.  This cut of beef in normally dry in my experience, but this was not the case at Ben's.  Whether the coffee rub, or the time in the smoker, this thin sliced pound of nearly black carne was just so moist, tender and delicious.  The taste of brisket was very present, but the secret sauce brought out undertones and texture that truly opened our eyes.  Even the normal stringiness of the cut was an asset on the platter.  It made for more surface area to hold the smoke and rub.  Can't say that I actually tasted coffee, but that wasn't needed to find this dish remarkable.  

There are a few downsides to eating at Ben's.  First, service was slow by definition.  Only one person doing everything.  She made a few mistakes on our orders, but nothing so egregious as to require markdowns.  Then, we were given plastic utensils to negotiate the load of food.  They simply were not up to the task of dealing with the meat and sides.  Broken fork prongs, snapped knives were a part of the night.  How much better to invest in real steel blades and spikes to control the contest.  As mentioned above, they seemed to be out of many of their listed brews. 

Prices are fair for the menu and (lack of) atmosphere.  

Put the smokers out in the parking lot for all to see, maintain your beer inventory, and provide customers with the tools to subdue the wild animals on our plates, and Ben (Franklin)'s could become a great BBQ mainstay in this area.

I found myself here for lunch and dinner one day last week due to a long court appearance.  I have no complaints about the kitchen, nor the service of Spice Thai Cuisine. 

The space is all cool dark wood and deep red texture that took me far away from the courthouse for a peaceful interlude.  The young server was gracious, engaging and had a high watt smile that made ordering a pleasure.  I asked if this was truly a Thai house, and she assured me the owner and chef were legit.  

For lunch I had the Hot Jungle Special at heat level 4 (out of 7).  The plate arrived loaded with fresh veggies and a mildly pepper/curry sauce that brought everything together nicely, but wasn't quite the inferno I was looking for.  Still, it was totally enjoyable, and I used it as a measure should I chose to return for another round.  That I returned for dinner was totally unexpected, unless you consider leaving a briefcase behind as an act of kismet.  I had to return that evening to get it, and while there decided to sit for dinner. 

I supped on Pad Thai with Calamari and heat level 5. This was more like it!  The meal arrived in a large ceramic plate with a built in pedestal.  It looked beautiful.  The spice level was excellent, and the Calamari was fresh and scored in a crosshatch pattern to expose max surface area.  It was soft and pliant.  The overall experience was delicious. I took enough home for another dinner.

Spice Thai Cuisine is a very good restaurant, if not quite at the level of Aroi Thai or some of the other specialty houses in the area.  No doubt, it could reach that apex with a little more time and imagination.

Wandered in after court one morning, needing coffee and something, having skipped breakfast to get out the door early.  Lily's was sitting there, cute windows suggesting something different inside. Wooden floors, large chalk board menus, dessert displayed right where they can do the most damage to good intentions.  And, bagels that looked more like they were from a ring toss game with sesame seeds and onion flakes.  Had to have it!
Fresh, chewy and flavorful.  Good coffee. Yes, and lemon bars that squeeze the salivaries into submission with a crunchy smooth sweet tartness. 
I walked out thinking this was a cool place; well worth another try, and wishing Lily's was in Newtown.

Great Harvest Bread Company sits in the same large Village of Newtown Shopping Center where McCaffery's now is. On impulse I went in this morning to see what was available for breakfast.  The friendly assistant bakery/counter person told me the muffins were still in the oven, but they had very fresh Blueberry Cream Cheese Scones available.  She pointed to them and allowed me to come around the counter to have a closer look (and take a photo).  

I don't know much about scones, except for eating them a few years ago when in England.  I remembered a hard, cookie-like outside and a textured chew.  These were quite different. They were the shape of scones, and soft through and through. No crunch. Much like a muffin in the shape of a scone. I liked it, the same as I would have enjoyed the muffin. Perhaps they were less sweet than their cousins. 

The loaves of bread were tempting, and I will try some of them over time.  The coffee was good, the beans roasted locally.  

Their wall menu suggests that their sandwiches are worth trying, as does the video attached to this Yelp listing.  

I look forward to future visits and sampling more of what appears to be high end healthy bread and all things that can be created out of it.  

Very happy to have them in Newtown.

I found Kriscroix while cruising Yelp for a change of pace meal in the area. Yesterday, I finally had the time to go there for an early lunch after dropping son off at the mall for a Magic tournament (that's another story). 

On first approach it is easy to miss this place on the end of a small strip on the south side of a particularly ugly stretch of Rt. 1 in Fairless Hills. The signage is small, and first glance is of a store that looks like a beer distributor, with many brew signs on the windows.  Don't be deterred.  Walk in, turn left, and you are in a 1970's dining room with comfortable blue leatherette booths, brass fitting, and wall to wall maritime memorabilia.  Very seaworthy!

I was fortunate to have Tracy as my server.  She was friendly, funny, and took time and pride to show me through the menu and make useful suggestions.  From the reviews I knew I was going to have good choices, but decided to go with the standard Fish and Chips for my first taste.
